title: Can You Max Out a 401(k) and IRA in the Same Year?
metaDescription: Yes, you can max out a 401(k) and IRA in the same year. See the separate limits, a contribution order, paycheck math, and income rules to check.
h1: Can You Max Out a 401(k) and IRA in the Same Year?
cardBlurb: The separate contribution limits, a practical savings order, and the income rules that can affect your IRA choice.
introText:
Yes, you can max out a [401(k)](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/401k-plans) and an [individual retirement account (IRA)](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-ira-contribution-limits) in the same year. Contributions to one do not reduce the other's limit.

For 2026, the 401(k) employee deferral limit is $24,500, or $32,500 with the age-50-plus catch-up under this site's convention. The IRA limit is set separately each year. Check the current IRA figure before deciding how much to send from each paycheck.

sections.heading: 401(k) and IRA Limits Are Separate
sections.body:
You can contribute up to the applicable employee limit in a 401(k) and up to the applicable IRA limit in the same year. Putting $1,000 into an IRA does not leave you with $1,000 less room in your 401(k). The accounts have separate limits, so you can plan each contribution on its own schedule.

The 2026 401(k) employee deferral limit is $24,500. Under this site's age-50-plus catch-up convention, that amount rises to $32,500. An employer match does not count against either figure: the limit described here applies to money you defer from your own pay. Keep the match separate when you calculate how much of your personal 401(k) limit remains.

The IRA figure needs a year check. The [Internal Revenue Service (IRS) IRA contribution limits page](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-ira-contribution-limits) listed $7,000 for 2025, but that is a 2025 figure. Verify the applicable limit for the year you are planning rather than carrying $7,000 into a 2026 budget by default. Your IRA contribution also cannot exceed your taxable compensation if your compensation is lower than the annual limit.

Reaching both limits requires enough money to fund them, but neither account takes away contribution room from the other. Start with the 2026 401(k) amount, add the verified IRA amount for 2026, and compare the total with what you can set aside during the year. Treat any employer match as additional money when you review the result, rather than counting it as part of your own contribution.

sections.heading: 401(k) and IRA Contribution Order
sections.body:
A common contribution order is to get the full employer match, fund an IRA, return to the 401(k), and then consider a taxable account. Start by finding the employee contribution needed to receive the full match available under your workplace plan. Contributing less than that amount leaves part of the available match unclaimed.

Next, decide whether a Roth or traditional IRA fits your tax situation. Your choice may depend on whether a traditional contribution is deductible and whether your income permits a direct Roth contribution. The [Roth IRA vs. traditional IRA comparison](/compare/roth-ira-vs-traditional-ira/) can help you make that choice before you set an automatic transfer. You do not have to finish funding the IRA before making another 401(k) contribution; the order is a way to set priorities when money is limited.

After setting an IRA target, raise your 401(k) deferral toward the $24,500 employee limit for 2026, or $32,500 under the age-50-plus catch-up convention. A taxable brokerage account comes after the retirement-account targets in this common order. If you are weighing those two destinations, the [401(k) vs. brokerage account comparison](/compare/401k-vs-brokerage-account/) explains the account differences.

Change the order if the tax rules make your preferred IRA contribution less useful or unavailable. For example, someone whose income limits a traditional IRA deduction may want to compare the remaining IRA choices with further 401(k) contributions before setting a transfer. The [401(k) vs. Roth IRA comparison](/compare/401k-vs-roth-ira/) is a starting point for that decision. The employer-match step remains the place to begin.

sections.heading: Traditional IRA Deductibility with a Workplace Plan
sections.body:
Maxing out a 401(k) does not, by itself, prevent you from contributing to a traditional IRA. The separate question is whether you can deduct the IRA contribution. If you or your spouse are covered by a workplace retirement plan, the deduction can be limited or phased out when income exceeds the applicable IRS thresholds.

That distinction matters when you compare accounts. An IRA contribution and an IRA deduction are different questions: first ask whether you can contribute, then ask whether the contribution qualifies for the deduction you expect. Do not assume a traditional IRA deposit will lower your tax bill simply because the IRA accepts the money. Review the [IRS IRA contribution limits and deduction information](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-ira-contribution-limits) for the year you are funding.

Coverage through a spouse's workplace plan can matter even if you are making the IRA contribution yourself. That makes a household income check useful before you choose a traditional IRA as the second step in your savings order. You do not need to guess an income cutoff from an older article; use the IRS figures for the contribution year.

If the deduction you expected is limited, revisit where the next dollar goes. You can compare an IRA with an additional 401(k) deferral, subject to your remaining employee limit. You can also review whether a direct Roth IRA contribution is available at your income. Set the automatic IRA transfer after that check, so the transfer follows the account choice you meant to make.

sections.heading: Roth IRA Income Limits and Account Choice
sections.body:
A Roth IRA can be part of a plan to max out both accounts, but direct Roth IRA contributions phase out at higher incomes. Check the [IRS Roth IRA rules](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/roth-iras) for the year of your contribution before treating the IRA limit as an amount you can put into a Roth IRA. The annual IRA limit and your eligibility to contribute directly to a Roth IRA are separate checks.

Income rules can change the middle of the common contribution order. Someone who expected to fund a Roth IRA may need to reconsider that step if their income is within or above the applicable phaseout range. Someone considering a traditional IRA should separately check whether a deduction is available. Neither income check reduces the 2026 401(k) employee deferral limit stated above.

Do not confuse a Roth IRA with a Roth 401(k) when you review your choices. They are different account types, so an IRA income rule should not be applied to a 401(k) decision without checking the relevant rules. The [Roth IRA vs. Roth 401(k) comparison](/compare/roth-ira-vs-roth-401k/) lays out the distinction if both appear in your savings plan.

Make the account decision before dividing an annual target into monthly transfers. Otherwise, you could build a budget around a direct Roth IRA contribution and later find that the income rule changes your plan. Check the current IRS Roth rules, choose the IRA contribution you can make, and then work out the amount per transfer.

sections.heading: Per-Paycheck Math for Maxing Both Accounts
sections.body:
To reach the 2026 401(k) employee limit over 26 equal paychecks, you would defer about $942.31 per paycheck. The calculation is $24,500 divided by 26. Under the $32,500 age-50-plus catch-up convention, the same calculation is $1,250 per paycheck. These figures describe your contributions; an employer match is additional and does not reduce the employee amount you may defer.

An IRA transfer takes a separate calculation because its limit must be verified for the year. Once you have that figure, divide it by 12 for a monthly target or by 26 if you prefer to set money aside each biweekly payday. For scale, the $7,000 IRA limit stated for 2025 works out to about $583.33 a month or $269.23 across 26 paychecks. Those are illustrations using the 2025 IRA figure, not a statement of the 2026 limit.

To see whether you can afford both targets, subtract your regular expenses from your expected take-home pay and compare the remainder with the IRA transfer. Account for the 401(k) deferral in your payroll plan rather than subtracting it twice. If the numbers do not fit, keep the full-match contribution as your first target and choose a smaller IRA transfer you can maintain.

A late start changes the paycheck math. If you have ten paychecks left and still want to contribute $5,000 more to your 401(k), the required deferral is $500 per paycheck. Apply the same remaining-target calculation to the IRA, then check both figures against your available pay. A target that fits over 26 paychecks may be too large when only ten remain.

sections.heading: Mistakes That Distort a Two-Account Plan
sections.body:
The easiest planning mistake is using the wrong year's IRA limit beside the 2026 401(k) limit. The $7,000 IRA figure in this page belongs to 2025. Look up the applicable IRA figure for the year you intend to contribute, then put both year labels next to your targets. This keeps a planning example from becoming an accidental contribution instruction.

Another mistake is counting an employer match as part of your $24,500 employee deferral limit. Keep a record of your own payroll contributions and track the match separately. If your goal is to max out your employee contributions, subtract only your employee deferrals from that employee limit. The same distinction applies when using the $32,500 age-50-plus figure under this site's convention.

A third mistake is treating IRA eligibility, Roth eligibility, and traditional IRA deductibility as the same test. Your IRA contribution cannot exceed your taxable compensation if that amount is below the annual IRA limit. Higher income can also phase out a direct Roth contribution, while workplace-plan coverage and income can limit a traditional IRA deduction. Check each rule that applies to the account you chose; passing one test does not answer the others.

Finally, do not let an annual target hide an unaffordable paycheck deduction. Divide your remaining goal by the paychecks left, not by the paychecks you originally expected to have. If the result crowds out necessary expenses, lower the contribution target. You can still follow a contribution order without reaching every annual limit.

sections.heading: A Plan When You Cannot Max Out Both
sections.body:
If you cannot afford both limits, contribute enough to your 401(k) to receive the full employer match first. Find that required contribution under your workplace plan and set a payroll deferral you can sustain. After that, choose an IRA amount that fits your budget rather than treating the annual IRA limit as a required payment.

Suppose you can save $300 a month after making the 401(k) contribution needed for the full match. Twelve $300 IRA transfers would add up to $3,600 over a year. You could use that as an IRA target, subject to the applicable annual limit, taxable-compensation cap, and account-specific income rules. A smaller recurring amount gives you a plan you can follow without claiming that you have maxed the IRA.

If your income limits the traditional IRA deduction or phases out direct Roth IRA contributions, check the applicable IRS rules before sending the $300. You may decide to put more toward your 401(k) instead, as long as you have employee deferral room left. The contribution order is useful only when its IRA step fits the contribution you can make and the tax result you expect.

You can revisit the numbers if your pay or expenses change. Calculate the remaining 401(k) employee room from your payroll contributions, then calculate the IRA room using the verified limit for that year and contributions already made. To see whether you can max out a 401(k) and IRA, divide each remaining target by the pay periods left and [verify the current IRA limit with the IRS](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-ira-contribution-limits).

faqs.question: Can I contribute the maximum to a 401(k) and an IRA in the same year?
faqs.answer: Yes. The 401(k) employee deferral limit and the IRA contribution limit are separate, so contributing to one does not reduce the other's limit. Check the IRA limit for the year you are funding and any income rules that apply to your chosen IRA.

faqs.question: Does my employer match count toward my 401(k) employee limit?
faqs.answer: No. The employer match does not count against your own employee deferral limit. Track your payroll deferrals separately when measuring progress toward the $24,500 limit for 2026, or $32,500 under this site's age-50-plus catch-up convention.

faqs.question: Should I max out my 401(k) or IRA first?
faqs.answer: A common order starts with enough 401(k) contributions to get the full employer match. Then consider an IRA, return to the 401(k) toward its employee limit, and consider a taxable account afterward. Check traditional IRA deduction rules and Roth IRA income rules before setting the IRA contribution.

faqs.question: Can I deduct a traditional IRA contribution if I have a 401(k)?
faqs.answer: Possibly, but the deduction can be limited or phased out if you or your spouse are covered by a workplace plan and your income exceeds IRS thresholds. A 401(k) does not by itself eliminate your ability to contribute to a traditional IRA. Check the deduction rules for the year of your contribution.

faqs.question: What if my income is too high for a direct Roth IRA contribution?
faqs.answer: Direct Roth IRA contributions phase out at higher incomes. Check the IRS rules for the year you want to contribute before scheduling a transfer. You can then review whether further 401(k) contributions or another account choice fits your situation.

faqs.question: How much should I save per paycheck to max out my 401(k) in 2026?
faqs.answer: Across 26 equal paychecks, $24,500 is about $942.31 per paycheck. Using the $32,500 age-50-plus catch-up figure under this site's convention, it is $1,250 per paycheck. If you start partway through the year, divide your remaining target by the paychecks left instead.
